title: James Bond has finally been cast. Now it’s time to pick the villains
text:
James Bond villains: Who could be cast as Robert Pattinson’s evil counterpart? Now it’s time to pick the villains
 By Nell Geraets , Meg Watson , Elizabeth Flux , Debbie Cuthbertson , Chris Hook and Garry Maddox November 21, 2026 Potential Bond villains (clockwise from left) Willem Defoe, Jesse Plemons, Kristen Stewart and Inde Navarrette. Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

 Close Share A A A Every James Bond needs an iconic villain. Sean Connery had Gert Fröbe as Auric Goldfinger, Roger Moore had Michael Lonsdale’s Hugo Drax. One foe, Ernst Stavro Blofeld , was so evil that he terrorised not one, but four Bonds (though he’s technically unnamed against Moore).
 With the long-awaited casting of Robert Pattinson as the next 007 , the search is on for his scheming counterpart. Could the upcoming film’s director Denis Villeneuve finally cast a female big-bad, no longer relegating women to the role of wily henchman or heartthrob seductress? Whether they’re a ruthless power broker, an unpredictable rogue or some dangerous AI enthusiast, one thing is certain: they will stop at nothing to kill the man in the tux.
 Loading 
 No casting has yet been confirmed, leaving the door wide open for this masthead’s Culture team to cast our best (and most chaotic) predictions. We were, admittedly, off the mark in our Bond speculations . Perhaps we’ll have more luck with the villains.
 Nell Geraets, culture reporter
 The beauty of casting a little freak like Pattinson as Bond is that Villeneuve can now go full-throttle on an unhinged villain. Who could possibly match the sparkling vampire skin, brooding Batman weirdness of Pattinson, you may ask? I have one name for you: Jesse Plemons.
 This guy takes bizarre to the next level. Not only does he have the kind of face that somehow looks simultaneously cherubic and unnerving, he’s also proven he has the acting chops to match it. In Bugonia , he convincingly plays a conspiracy-obsessed beekeeper who kidnaps a woman he thinks is an alien.
 Advertisement Related Article
 James Bond 
 Robert Pattinson cast as next James Bond 
 In Civil War , he’s a cold-blooded militia soldier with the strangest taste in sunglasses. And don’t even get me started on his sick, twisted character in Black Mirror ’s fourth season . His previous work demonstrates that Plemons can easily slip into villainy and instability in equal measure. Pattinson’s Bond needs this kind of unsettling unpredictability to truly cook as what I hope will be our first “weird Bond”.
 My wildcard, however, is Pierce Brosnan . Before you accuse me of desecrating the Bond franchise (a former James Bond trying to kill James Bond – gasp!), hear me out. Not only would Brosnan’s villain be so deliciously meta, he would also arguably be the smoothest criminal mastermind known to man. He already showed off his immaculate suaveness as 007, so just imagine that poise combined with a bit of bloodlust – sign me straight up.
 Chris Hook, culture news editor
 Let’s be bold. Just as Daniel Craig’s emotionally vulnerable, self-aware Bond was reflective of Gen X, and the social change around gender that came with that cohort, Pattinson could be the flagbearer for a new era.
 Instead of a Bond girl, why not go for a Bond boy as the romantic interest, with a female villain? Pattinson has a wonderfully fluid sexual energy (maybe it’s a vampire thing?) – the writers should lean in and have fun with it.
 Kristen Stewart in Love Lies Bleeding. Anna Kooris/A24 via AP Advertisement Imagine, Bond falls for the right-hand man of the scheming female villain, who must absolutely be played by Kristen Stewart, (evil tech mogul for sure). We definitely don’t need another bloke hamming it up as the antagonist.
 While technically a Millennial, Pattinson has insisted over the years that he has Gen Z habits and a zedder vibe – this would absolutely cement that claim and open up future Bond plots to some very different and unpredictable storytelling.
 I can already sense a trembling in the anti-woke obsessive subconscious hive mind. For their reaction alone, it’d be worth it.
 Elizabeth Flux, arts editor, The Age 
 Here is what I would like to see happen: Robert Pattinson v Robert Pattinson. And I don’t mean in a psychological James-Bond-contains-multitudes-is-he-his-own-worst-enemy kind of way. I mean quite literally I want him to separately play James Bond and the film’s villain.
 It could be an evil twin situation. It could be a clone thing. It would be a bit boring if it’s a robot made to look like him which learns from his behaviour as a way to make AI the true villain, but I’d accept it (even though Mission Impossible already did AI as the villain). Maybe it could be that Bond is chosen for the mission because he resembles the villain and embeds himself in his enemy’s life. Endless possibilities! It would be fun. But, also, maybe let’s save that for his second (or third) film.
 Advertisement Cillian Murphy as Pattinson’s villainous counterpart? Yes, please. For his first film, it’s a coin toss between Cillian Murphy and Inde Navarrette. Murphy feels like the obvious choice and that’s fair because he is excellent in everything he does – his performance as Scarecrow in The Dark Knight Trilogy is just as chilling on re-watch as it was when I first saw it. Inde Navarrette is the less obvious choice, but if you’ve seen her in Obsession you know she would do something interesting and truly frightening. 
 Meg Watson, deputy television editor
 I’m fully on board with the Jesse Plemons and Cillian Murphy campaigns, but here’s another name for the fun of it: Michael Sheen. This talented Welshman was rumoured to be in the running to play Blofield (the super villain who inspired Dr Evil) back in 2009, and he’s only strengthened his case since.
 Michael Sheen as Roland Blum in The Good Fight. Patrick Harbron/CBS A legend of the stage and screen, as comfortable performing Shakespeare as he is geeing up the Welsh rugby team , Sheen commands authority and slips into villainy with manic glee.
 A few years back he transfixed audiences at the Sydney Opera House as Salieri in Amadeus ; a performance the Herald’s reviewer called “dazzling”, inspiring us to “cheer his evil” . I had a similar experience watching him as Roland Blum, a bombastic and often sickening Trumpian lawyer in The Good Fight who was praised as the “wild id” of the show.

 These are the kind of grade-A kooky performances that could hold their own against whatever Robert Pattinson serves up as Bond. And that’s without even getting into the fact that Sheen’s already proved himself a master spy hunter in this year’s Celebrity Traitors .
 Debbie Cuthbertson, culture news editor
 Robert Pattinson’s former Twilight co-star Kristen Stewart would be a brilliant baddie – I’d love to see her face off against him as a Bond villain, she’d be a great foil to his 007.
 Stewart has had such an interesting career post- Twilight in indie and arthouse films. Just like Pattinson, she’s made some fascinating and unexpected choices in the roles she has taken on, from Diana in Pablo Larraín’s Spencer to Kelly Reichardt’s Certain Women and Olivier Assayas’ haunting films Personal Shopper and Clouds of Sils Maria .
 And just their history together, as former Twilight co-stars in another big franchise – and their past relationship – would make that a really delicious pairing.
 My other preferred candidate for Bond villain is Willem Dafoe. He would eat up a role like that, and it would be a great way to reunite him with Pattinson after they faced off together in the deeply disturbing Robert Eggers film The Lighthouse .
 Advertisement Willem Dafoe in The Lighthouse. A24 Films Garry Maddox, senior writer
 Acclaimed European actors have made great Bond villains over the past two decades, led by Mads Mikkelsen ( Casino Royale ), Javier Bardem ( Skyfall ) and Christoph Waltz ( Spectre , No Time To Die ), with American Rami Malek also strong in No Time To Die .
 Director Denis Villeneuve has always gone for diverse casts and strong roles for women. So, I’m expecting the new Bond villain will be, firstly, a quality actor and, secondly, a contrast to Robert Pattinson as 007.
 Yahya Abdul-Mateen II would make a great foil to Robert Pattinson’s 007. Universal That means he or she will probably not be white, probably not English and possibly not around the same age (40-ish).
 The better the villain, the better the hero, so an actor who has an edge – who can convincingly play intelligent and cruel – works. While the actor needs to fit the script rather than the other way around, I’d be considering the likes of Benicio del Toro, Sandra Hüller, Stellan Skarsgård, Yahya Abdul-Mateen II, Salma Hayek and Joaquin Phoenix.
